column1: # What CI does with each root-workspace package clippy still refuses.
# columns: status
# `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` is printed at
# README.md:183 and its deny table lives at Cargo.toml:119, and until
# `tools/ci/run.sh clippy` existed NO TIER RAN IT -- the table was enforced by a
# human typing that line. 1bdf5572f found a red that had survived a day, and
# named this as the debt it was evidence of.
# THE FIRST FULL CENSUS, at the commit that added this file, found reds in 44 of
# 105 workspace members, and 69 members that clippy NEVER REACHED because a
# package they depend on was red -- `--keep-going` builds what it can and stops
# at a red lib, so a red kernel hides everything above it. That is why this file
# is a debt list and not a quarantine of individual lints: the unit that matters
# is the PACKAGE, because a red package is what blinds the tier.
# STATUS:
#   debt        is RED today and must STAY red. A `debt` package that goes GREEN
#               fails this tier BY NAME -- the fix landed and the row is now
#               stale coverage. Delete the row in the commit that fixed it.
#               Every other package must be clean; a red one with no row here
#               fails the tier, which is the ratchet.
# THE `sites` NUMBER IS NOT A GATE and is deliberately not compared. It is the
# size of the debt when the row was written, so a reader can see whether a row
# is one line or fifty without running anything. The gate is the package's
# red/green, which cannot drift.
# `owner` is the LAST COMMIT to touch the file, and its `Lane:` trailer where it
# has one. Commits before 2026-09-02 carry no trailer (`tools/lane.sh` began
# writing it that day), so an older row names a commit and not a lane. It is a
# starting point for whoever picks the row up, not an accusation.
# WHY THESE WERE NOT FIXED IN THE SAME COMMIT, in one sentence each, in the note
# column. Three shapes recur: a live lane holds the file (the CI lane does not
# edit another lane's working file), the lint is a design question whose answer
# is not a lint fix, or the finding is a REAL DEFECT that belongs to whoever
# knows the code -- `dead_code` on a test function is a test that does not run,
# and no lint lane should decide whether to delete it or wire it up.
